h1: The 4 Best Toaster Ovens Under $50 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Toaster Ovens Under $50: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: four toaster ovens that stay under $50, compared on slice capacity, interior volume, wattage and counter footprint.
summary: The Elite Gourmet ETO449X is the best toaster oven under $50: 4 slices, 800W, an 8.99L interior and a pizza function in the $25 to $50 bucket. The ETO490 lists a slightly larger 9L interior but no wattage. The Dash Mini is the cheapest, under $25, and the ETO236 is the 2-slice option for tiny counters.
intro: Cheap toaster ovens trip buyers in one predictable way: they count slices, order the 2-slice model, and find that the quarter sheet or frozen pizza they own will not go in. Under $50 there is little brand prestige to pay for. What separates one box from another is interior size, wattage and whether the listing bothers to tell you either.

We kept only models whose price bucket sits entirely under $50, which left four, and ranked them from their spec sheets on capacity, interior volume, wattage and extras. Pricier ovens were left out even when they looked tempting. Most listings here are thin, so a model that names more of its own numbers scores higher than one that stays silent.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO449X Toaster Oven
products.verdict: The most complete spec sheet under $50.
products.description:
The Elite Gourmet ETO449X is a 4-slice oven with an 800W element, an 8.99L interior and a pizza function, in the $25 to $50 bucket. Wattage is the number that tells you how much heating power sits behind the door. It drives how quickly a small cavity preheats and how well it recovers when you open it. Most ovens in this price range do not publish it.

It takes first place because its listing names capacity, wattage, volume and a pizza setting at once. The ETO490 lists a marginally larger 9L interior, but without wattage or the pizza detail. The Dash Mini is cheaper but names even less.

Buy it if you want one small oven for toast and the occasional frozen pizza. The caveat is that the listing gives few other details, such as rack positions or timer range. Measure the interior against your pan before ordering, and skip it if you need a large pan or convection.
products.idealFor: Small households wanting toast and frozen pizza.
products.skipIf: You need a large pan or convection.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO490 9L/4-Slice Oven
products.verdict: A 9L, 4-slice oven aimed at busier households.
products.description:
The Elite Gourmet ETO490 lists a 4-slice capacity and a 9L interior in the $25 to $50 bucket, and the 9L figure is the largest interior on this list. That is a hair above the ETO449X's 8.99L, which is a difference of 0.01L and not something a cook will notice on a tray. Both sit in the same small class of oven, so neither is a replacement for a full-size range.

It ranks just below the ETO449X because its listing does not name a wattage or a pizza setting. That is the only real spec gap between the two, so your decision comes down to whether you want the extra information and the pizza function or accept silence for the 9L label.

Buy it for a busy household that toasts every day, which is how the maker positions it. The caveat is the thin sheet: confirm the wattage on the listing before you pay. Skip it if you need a listed power figure or a pizza mode.
products.skipIf: You want a listed wattage or pizza mode.

products.name: Dash Mini Toaster Oven
products.verdict: The least expensive oven here, with a pizza function.
products.description:
The Dash Mini is a compact toaster oven with a pizza function, and it is the only pick under $25. A mini oven earns its place where a full 4-slice box would crowd a shelf: a dorm, a first apartment, a rented room with a single outlet. The pizza function is the one extra the listing names.

It ranks third because it lists no slice capacity, no wattage and no volume, unlike the Elite Gourmet models above. That silence is a risk: you cannot tell whether a 9 inch pie, a pair of bagels or a small tray will fit. In return it costs the least, which is the whole tradeoff against the ETO449X.

Buy it for a dorm shelf or a first apartment when price comes first. The caveat is the short spec sheet, so check the listed interior size for your needs. Skip it if you need clear capacity details before buying.
products.idealFor: Dorm rooms and first apartments on a tight budget.

products.name: Elite Gourmet ETO236 Compact 2-Slice Toaster Oven
products.verdict: A 2-slice oven for counters with no room to spare.
products.description:
The Elite Gourmet ETO236 is a compact 2-slice toaster oven in the $25 to $50 bucket. It is the smallest oven here, and that small body matters in a tiny galley kitchen or on a counter shared with a coffee maker. Its listing names the slice count and nothing else: no wattage, no volume, no extras.

It ranks last because two slices is the smallest capacity on the list. Compared with the 4-slice ETO449X and ETO490, you save footprint but lose the ability to toast four slices or warm a small tray. At a similar price, the larger models give you more room for the same money.

Buy it if you cook for yourself and counter space is scarce. The caveat is that a 2-slice oven will not hold larger pans, so skip it if you cook for more than one or two people. Confirm interior dimensions before you order.
products.idealFor: Solo cooks with very limited counter space.

whatMatters.detail: Slice count is the maker's shorthand for interior width. A 4-slice oven handles more bread or a small tray, while a 2-slice oven is easier to store. Check the listing for both slice count and interior volume rather than relying on one, since a 4-slice label does not guarantee a pan will fit. Measure the pan you actually own.

Volume in liters shows how much food fits at once. The ETO490 lists 9L and the ETO449X lists 8.99L, which is close enough to treat as equal. Look for the figure in the bullet points and compare it with the pan or tray you own; a liter count beats any slice claim. A missing volume, as with the Dash Mini and ETO236, is a red flag worth asking about.

Wattage shows how much heating power the element has, which affects how quickly the oven preheats and how steady it holds temperature. Only the ETO449X lists 800W here. Look for it in the specs before assuming performance, and treat a missing number as a gap, not a promise. Higher wattage generally means faster preheat.

A pizza setting adapts the heating for frozen pizza, so the crust cooks without scorching the top. Both the Dash Mini and the ETO449X list one. Check the listing wording rather than assuming a dial label, and confirm the interior is wide enough for the pizza size you buy.

A toaster oven takes counter space and needs clearance on the sides and top for heat. The 2-slice ETO236 is the smallest here. Measure your counter and compare it with the listed dimensions, and leave a few inches behind the unit for the cord and air movement. Never push it against a wall.

faq.q: Will a 4-slice oven fit a full-size pizza?
faq.a: No spec in the listings says so. The ETO449X lists a pizza function and an 8.99L interior, so expect smaller frozen pizzas and confirm dimensions first. The ETO490 and Dash Mini list no pizza dimensions either, so measure before you order, using the box dimension and not just the slice label.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake?
faq.a: Buying on slice count alone. Compare interior volume as well, since the ETO490 lists 9L and the ETO449X lists 8.99L. Then check wattage, which only the ETO449X names, at 800W, and whether a pizza function is listed.

faq.q: Is a pricier oven worth it?
faq.a: If you want convection or air frying, yes, but those models sit above $50. For basic toasting and a frozen pizza, the ETO449X or ETO490 is enough, and the Dash Mini covers the lowest budgets with a basic pizza function.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Place it on a flat counter with clearance around the sides and top. Read the manual for the pizza function if your model has one, such as the ETO449X or Dash Mini, and run it empty briefly.

faq.q: How do I clean a small toaster oven?
faq.a: Unplug it, let it cool, and wipe the interior and crumbs out of the tray. Check the manual for removable parts. A weekly crumb check matters more on the ETO490 if it gets daily use, because crumbs left behind can smoke.

None of the four lists convection. The ETO449X, ETO490, Dash Mini and ETO236 all use a basic setup, and convection models sit above $50. Expect a simple heated-box oven that toasts and reheats, not one that crisps like an air fryer.

finalTake: Buy the ETO449X if you want one small oven that names its wattage, volume and pizza setting. Take the ETO490 for a bigger listed interior, the Dash Mini when price is everything, and the ETO236 only for a solo cook with almost no counter. None lists convection, so step above $50 if you want it.
